name: AIKeyboard emoji search corpus
notes: Frozen judging corpus for `EmojiSearch`. Each entry is one query typed into the emoji search box, in one of the two languages this keyboard types, plus a human judgement about what a good answer would be.
`query` is the raw string, before `EmojiSearch.normalise` touches it. A few entries deliberately carry case or padding so the normalising step is exercised rather than assumed.
`intended` is the one emoji a person typing this query meant. It is judged on **position**, not presence: rank 1 is a hit, rank 17 is not. Present only where one answer is obviously the answer.

`acceptable` is the set of emoji that would be a good first answer where more than one would be. `acceptableIsClosed` true means the list is meant to be complete and anything else in rank 1 is wrong; false means the slot is genuinely open and the list is a sample of good answers, never a whitelist.
`acceptableSource` is on every entry that carries a list, so it can never be mistaken for something an engine returned.

**`intended` and `acceptable` never appear on the same entry.** Where one emoji is the answer and others are near it, the near ones are written as `alsoFine` — human-authored like `acceptable`, printed by the scorer, and never counted either way. Mixing the two would have made `targetRank` mean the rank of something other than the thing being judged, which is how an entry ends up reading as a pass and a fail at once.

`mustNotRank` is reserved for emoji of a **different concept** that this query has pulled up or plausibly could: a carrot for `car`, a moon cake for `moon`. It is a failure wherever one appears inside `mustNotRankWindow` (5, the visible strip), regardless of what won rank 1. An emoji that is merely the less-wanted member of the right concept does not belong here — `intended` already says which one should be first.
`recent` is the recents list to pass in, present only on the entries that probe the recents boost. Absent means an empty recents list, which is what a fresh install has.
`expectEmpty` marks queries that must return nothing at all.
`knownGap` names an entry that is expected to fail today for a reason already understood and written down. It is still scored and still counted; it is not excused. Two entries carry it.

**Authored before any of it was run.** The query list and every `intended` / `acceptable` value were written from what a person typing that word means, not from what the ranker answers. Four queries are the exception and are marked with `priorKnowledge`: `heart`, `car`, `לב` and `moon` were already named in `.claude/docs/test-suite-state.md` with the engine's current answer, so those four could not be authored blind. The judgements written for them match the prose that was already in the repo, and a critic should discount them accordingly.

One entry, `en-run`, was widened *after* the first run and carries a `revised` field saying exactly what changed and why. It is the only one. Everything else in this file is what was written before a score existed, including the entries it turned out to fail.
Nothing here records what any engine returned. Measured output lives in results.json, which is dated.

categories.single-concept: One obvious answer and the query is close to its name.
categories.name-vs-keyword: The target's CLDR name is not the query, so the query reaches it as a keyword while other emoji reach it on a name. The `car` / `automobile` shape.
categories.ambiguous: Several emoji are all a fine answer. Judged on `acceptable`, not on one winner.
categories.prefix: A partial word, which is what the box sees on every keystroke before the last one.
categories.multiword: Two words. `EmojiSearch` splits names and keywords on spaces, so a two-word needle can only ever equal a whole name.
categories.normalisation: Case and padding, which `EmojiSearch.normalise` is responsible for.
categories.recents: The recents boost: it should win a close call and lose to a name.
categories.morphology: A Hebrew word form that is not the form CLDR carries.

entries.probes: The plainest emoji query there is. ❤️ is named 'red heart' and 🫀 is named 'anatomical heart', so both carry `heart` as an exact keyword and the tiebreak alone decides it. Nobody typing heart into a message means the organ.
entries.priorKnowledge: Named in .claude/docs/test-suite-state.md with the engine's current answer before this corpus was written.

entries.probes: 🚗 is named 'automobile', so no name rung reaches it at all, while 'carrot' and 'card index dividers' start with the query and 'police car' carries it as a whole word.
entries.priorKnowledge: Named in .claude/docs/test-suite-state.md with the engine's current answer before this corpus was written.

entries.probes: The query is the whole name. If this is not rank 1 nothing else in the file matters.
Named exactly 'fire'. The other half of the floor this corpus rests on.
🐕 is named 'dog' and 🐶 is 'dog face'. Either is right; a third animal is not.
Same shape as dog, and the control for the recents entry that uses it.
The commonest emoji in any chat app and not one of the three is named for the word.
'crying face' and 'loudly crying face' both start with the query on a name word.
A dozen faces carry 'smiling' and none is named 'smile', so this is decided entirely by the prefix rungs and the tiebreak.
Two words that are exactly a CLDR name, which is the only way a multi-word query can reach rung 0. The positive control for the two multi-word entries that cannot.
Two letters. Short needles match a great many prefixes, so this is where a prefix rung with no length discipline shows.
☀️ is named 'sun'. Sunrise, sunset, sunflower and sunglasses all start with it.
Eight phases plus a cake all carry the word. The crescent is what people mean by the moon emoji; 🥮 is a pastry.
entries.priorKnowledge: Named in .claude/docs/test-suite-state.md as an answer one of the two rejected repairs moved, before this corpus was written.

entries.probes: ⭐ is named 'star'. 'star-struck' is a face and 'starry' is weather.
'beer mug' and 'clinking beer mugs'. Both are beer; the mug is the one people send.
☕ is named 'hot beverage'; coffee is only a keyword. The same shape as `car`, on a word people type constantly.
🍰 is 'shortcake', 🎂 is 'birthday cake', 🧁 is 'cupcake', 🥮 is 'moon cake'. Three of those are what an English speaker means by cake.
The popper, the face and the confetti ball are the three a person means. A piñata is a party object and not the answer to the word.
'mobile phone', 'telephone', 'telephone receiver'. The mobile is the one a person under fifty means.
✈️ is named 'airplane', so the query is a keyword and a prefix of nothing.
'house' and 'house with garden' — the plain one covers the query fully and the other does not.
'money bag', 'money-mouth face', 'money with wings'. The bag is the one that means money.
'open book', 'books', 'closed book'. All three are books.
Three musical notes, none of them named 'music'.
Snowflake, snowman, cloud with snow. Any of them answers the word.
The rain cloud, the umbrella, the sun behind rain. Rainbow starts with the query and is not rain.
'woman dancing' and 'man dancing' are both named for dancing, not dance, so the query only ever reaches them as a keyword or a prefix.
A dozen flowers, none of them named 'flower'. Genuinely open.
'deciduous tree', 'evergreen tree', 'palm tree'. All three carry it as a whole word of a two-word name, so coverage alone separates them.
Named exactly 'baby', with baby bottle, baby chick and baby angel around it.
🎁 is named 'wrapped gift', so the query is a whole word of a longer name rather than the name.
'angry face', 'enraged face', 'face with symbols on mouth'. The first is named for the word.
No emoji is named 'sad'; four carry it as a keyword. Nothing but the keyword rung can answer this.
The broadest emotional query there is, and every heart and half the faces carry it.
'sleeping face', 'zzz', 'person in bed' — the last two reach it only as a keyword.

🏃 is 'person running'. Three letters, so a great many prefixes match. The gendered runners are the same answer — this keyboard has no gender picker any more than it has a skin-tone one — so all three count, and a shoe does not.
entries.revised: Authored as `intended: 🏃` and widened after the first run, which answered 🏃‍♀️. The original was an authoring mistake rather than a ranker failure — I did not know the catalogue carried the gendered variants — but it was corrected with the output in front of me and a critic should discount it accordingly. It is the only entry in this file that was changed after being run.

entries.probes: 🚆 is named 'train'; the locomotive, the high-speed train and the tram all carry it too.
'soccer ball'. One right answer and no competition.
Three check marks, all named with the word.
Digits, not letters. 💯 is named 'hundred points' and carries `100` as a keyword, so this is the one query in the file that reaches its answer through a number.
🌊 is 'water wave'. The waving hand is named 'waving', which the query does not prefix, so this is not the ambiguity it looks like.
The cake is named for it; the balloon, the party face and the gift all carry it as a keyword.
'red apple' and 'green apple'. Red is the default fruit.
Named exactly 'rainbow', and its keyword list is long and political, which is a fair test that a long keyword list does not dilute a name match.
The flag people in this keyboard's market type most. Its name is 'flag: israel', so the query is a whole word of it.
A second flag, so the first is not the only evidence that flags are reachable.
Three keystrokes into pizza. The box searches on every keystroke, so most of what it ever ranks is a prefix.
Prefix of 'chocolate bar' on a name word.
Long enough to leave 'cup with straw' behind, which is what a short prefix would not do.
The keyboard capitalises the first letter of a field by default, so a capitalised query is the ordinary case rather than an edge one. The catalogue is lowercased by the generator.
A trailing space is one autocorrect commit away in any field. `normalise` trims.
The full CLDR name of the emoji this corpus argues about, so `heart` failing and `red heart` failing are tellable apart.

The Hebrew half of `heart`, and the entry that decides which of two contradicting Swift tests is right. 🫀's Hebrew CLDR name is the bare noun לב while its English name says 'anatomical' out loud, so the organ is marked in one locale and unmarked in the other. That is a shortcoming of the Hebrew annotation, not a difference in what people mean: a person typing לב into a chat wants the same red heart a person typing `heart` wants. See Bar/emoji/README.md.

entries.probes: 🔥's Hebrew name exactly. Two letters, so short-needle behaviour is on trial in Hebrew as well.
The Hebrew name of 🍕. The floor of the Hebrew side.
'דגל: ישראל'. The query is a whole word of the name, with the colon attached to the other one.
🙏 is named 'כפות ידיים מוצמדות' and reaches this only as a keyword. The commonest thing anybody sends.
🐕 is named כלב and 🐶 is פני כלב, the exact shape of the English `dog` entry.
Same shape again, so a Hebrew result that only works for one animal is visible.
☀️'s Hebrew name exactly, with several weather emoji carrying it inside longer names.
The Hebrew `car`, and arguably worse: 🌙's Hebrew name is סהר, so ירח reaches it only as a keyword, while 'ירח מלא', 'ירח חדש' and the cake 'עוגת ירח סינית' all carry it as a name word.
⭐'s Hebrew name exactly, against 'כוכב זוהר' and a face named 'פרצוף עם עיני כוכבים'.
'כוס בירה' and 'השקת כוסות בירה'. Neither is named the bare word, so this is a whole-word-inside-a-name contest.
☕ is 'משקה חם' in Hebrew as it is 'hot beverage' in English, so the everyday word is a keyword in both locales.
'פרוסת עוגה', 'עוגת יום הולדת', 'עוגה אישית' and the Chinese moon cake. Hebrew glues its construct forms, so עוגת is a different token from עוגה and only some of these match at all.
No party emoji is named מסיבה; several carry it as a keyword. The Hebrew half of `party`.
'טלפון נייד', 'טלפון רגיל', 'שפופרת טלפון'. The mobile is the one people mean.
✈️'s Hebrew name exactly, where the English side had to reach it as a keyword.
🏠 is named בית. It is also the first word of a great many Hebrew compounds — בית חולים, בית ספר — so a prefix rung with no discipline drowns it.
'שק כסף' and 'שטר דולר', which carries כסף as a keyword only.
'ספר פתוח', 'ספר סגור', 'ספרים'. The last is a prefix match rather than a whole word, which is the ordinary Hebrew plural and not an edge case.
None of the three notes is named for it; all carry it as a keyword. Hebrew also spells it two ways, and only one of them is here.
'ענן עם גשם', 'מטריה עם טיפות גשם', 'שמש מאחורי ענן עם גשם'. All three are rain.
'פתית שלג', 'איש שלג בלי שלג', 'ענן עם שלג'.
Most flowers carry פרח as a keyword and none is named it, so this is the Hebrew keyword rung under load.
'עץ נשיר', 'עץ ירוק-עד', 'עץ דקל' — three two-word names, so coverage alone separates them. Two letters again.
👶's Hebrew name exactly.
🎁 is 'קופסת מתנה'. A whole word of a two-word name, the same as the English `gift`.
'פרצוף כועס' is named for it; the others carry it as a keyword.
'פרצוף עצוב' is named for it, and several faces carry it as a keyword.
The Hebrew `love`: every heart and half the faces carry it.

The control half of `car`: this **is** 🚗's Hebrew name, so the Hebrew query reaches on rung 0 what the English query can only reach as a keyword. If this passes and `car` fails, the defect is the ranking and not the data.
'מתגלגל על הרצפה מרוב צחוק' carries it in a seven-word name, which is the longest name in this file and the hardest case for a coverage term.
Named in `EmojiSearch`'s own doc comment as the Hebrew form that works, so it is the control for the one below it.
The same root as בוכה in a different form. Matching is by whole word and by prefix, so nothing reaches it.
entries.knownGap: Hebrew morphology. `EmojiSearch`'s doc comment names this exact pair. Fixing it needs a stemmer the package does not have. Red on purpose; it is still counted.

entries.probes: One word, three meanings: the greeting, the peace symbol and the dove. All three are defensible and the greeting is what a chat field wants.
🌈 is 'קשת בענן', so the query is the first word of the name.
Three keystrokes into פיצה, the Hebrew half of `piz`.
Two Hebrew words. 🎂 is 'עוגת יום הולדת' and 🥳 carries 'יום הולדת' in its keywords, but keywords are split on spaces and no name equals the query, so a two-word Hebrew query has no rung to land on.
entries.knownGap: Multi-word queries can only reach rung 0, which needs a name equal to the whole query. The English `thumbs up` gets there and this cannot. Red on purpose; it is still counted.

entries.probes: The full Hebrew name of ❤️, so a Hebrew multi-word query that *does* equal a name is on the file next to one that does not.

The same query as he-lev with a realistic recents list. The right answer must not depend on whether ❤️ happens to be in recents — that is the difference between a ranker that is right and one that is propped up.
A genuine close call: 🐈 is named 'cat' and 🐱 is 'cat face', so recents should decide it. This is what the recents boost is for, on a pair whose tie is real rather than manufactured by a tiebreak bug.

The other half of the same close call. Whichever of the two is in recents should be first, and a pair is the only way to say that: one of these two entries must be doing real work no matter which way the ranker leans with an empty recents list.
Recents must lose to a name outright, or every query answers with whatever was sent last.
The same in Hebrew, because the boost is applied to a rung and rungs are earned differently in the two locales.
An earlier draft returned the whole catalogue for an empty needle and drew all 1,870 into the strip.
Empty after trimming, which is a different code path from empty on arrival.
No match anywhere. Note 💤 is named 'zzz', so a substring matcher would answer this and a prefix matcher must not.
The Hebrew half of the same question, so an empty result in one script is not the only evidence.
